In [[statistics]], '''separation''' is a phenomenon associated with models for [[Dichotomy|dichotomous]] or categorical outcomes, including [[logistic regression|logistic]] and [[probit regression]].  Separation occurs if the predictor (or a [[linear combination]] of some subset of the predictors) is associated with only one outcome value when the predictor range is split at a certain value.  

== The phenomenon ==
For example, if the predictor ''X'' is continuous, and the outcome ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 for all observed ''x''&nbsp;>&nbsp;2.  If the outcome values are (seemingly) perfectly determined by the predictor (e.g., ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 when ''x''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;2) then the condition "complete separation" is said to occur.  If instead there is some overlap (e.g., ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 when ''x''&nbsp;<&nbsp;2, but ''y'' has observed values of 0 and 1 when ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2) then "quasi-complete separation" occurs.  A [[contingency table|2&nbsp;×&nbsp;2 table]] with an empty (zero) cell is an example of quasi-complete separation.

== The problem ==
This observed form of the data is important because it sometimes causes problems with the estimation of regression coefficients. For example, [[maximum likelihood estimation|maximum likelihood (ML) estimation]] relies on maximization of the likelihood function, where e.g. in case of a [[logistic regression]] with completely separated data the maximum appears at the parameter space's margin, leading to "infinite" estimates, and, along with that, to problems with providing sensible [[standard error|standard errors]].<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Guoping |last1=Zeng |first2=Emily |last2=Zeng |title=On the Relationship between Multicollinearity and Separation in Logistic Regression |journal=[[Communications in Statistics]] |series=Simulation and Computation |year=2019 |volume=50 |issue=7 |pages=1989–1997 |doi=10.1080/03610918.2019.1589511 |s2cid=132047558 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Albert |first1=A. |last2=Anderson |first2=J. A. |year=1984 |title=On the Existence of Maximum Likelihood Estimates in Logistic Regression Models |journal=Biometrika |volume=71 |issue=1–10 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1093/biomet/71.1.1 }}</ref> Statistical software will often output an arbitrarily large parameter estimate with a very large standard error.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=B. D. |last1=McCullough |first2=H. D. |last2=Vinod |title=Verifying the Solution from a Nonlinear Solver: A Case Study |journal=[[American Economic Review]] |volume=93 |issue=3 |year=2003 |pages=873–892 |doi=10.1257/000282803322157133 |jstor=3132121 }}</ref>  

==Possible remedies==
An approach to "fix" problems with [[maximum likelihood estimation|ML estimation]] is the use of [[regularization (mathematics)|regularization]] (or "[[continuity correction|continuity corrections]]").<ref>{{citation|last1=Cole|first1=S.R.|last2=Chu|first2=H.|last3=Greenland|first3=S.|title=Maximum likelihood, profile likelihood, and penalized likelihood: A primer|journal=American Journal of Epidemiology|year=2014|volume=179|issue=2|pages=252–260|doi=10.1093/aje/kwt245|pmid=24173548 |pmc=3873110 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{citation|last1=Sweeting|first1=M.J.|last2=Sutton|first2=A.J.|last3=Lambert|first3=P.C.|title=What to add to nothing? Use and avoidance of continuity corrections in meta-analysis of sparse data|journal=Statistics in Medicine|year=2004|volume=23|issue=9|pages=1351–1375|doi=10.1002/sim.1761|pmid=15116347 |s2cid=247667708 }}</ref>
In particular, in case of a logistic regression problem, the use of ''exact logistic regression'' or ''Firth logistic regression'', a bias-reduction method based on a penalized likelihood, may be an option.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Mohammad Ali |last1=Mansournia |first2=Angelika |last2=Geroldinger |first3=Sander |last3=Greenland |author-link3=Sander Greenland |first4=Georg |last4=Heinze |title=Separation in Logistic Regression: Causes, Consequences, and Control |journal=[[American Journal of Epidemiology]] |volume=187 |issue=4 |year=2018 |pages=864–870 |doi=10.1093/aje/kwx299 |pmid=29020135 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Alternatively, one may avoid the problems associated with likelihood maximization by switching to a [[Bayesian inference|Bayesian]] approach to inference. Within a Bayesian framework, the pathologies arising from likelihood maximization are avoided by the use of [[integral|integration]] rather than [[mathematical optimization|maximization]], as well as by the use of sensible [[prior probability|prior probability distributions]].<ref>{{citation|last1=Gelman|first1=A.|last2=Jakulin|first2=A.|last3=Pittau|first3=M.G.|last4=Su|first4=Y.|title=A weakly informative default prior distribution dor logistic and other regression models|journal=Annals of Applied Statistics|year=2008|volume=2|issue=4|pages=1360–1383|doi=10.1214/08-AOAS191|doi-access=free|author1-link=Andrew Gelman |arxiv=0901.4011}}</ref>
